abstract: By predicting evolutionarily stable strategies of resource allocation between female and male functions under different ecological and genetic conditions, sex allocation theory aims to explain the diversity of reproductive systems within and among species. A fundamental limitation of this theory, however, is that it generally predicts evolutionarily stable discrete distributions of sexual phenotypes. In natural populations, by contrast, sexual phenotypes often exhibit continuous variation, ranging from pure male to pure female individuals. Here, we investigate the form of continuous stationary distributions of sexual phenotypes arising from mutation-selection balance. We extend classical models of sex allocation by incorporating recurrent, infinitesimal mutations, resulting in a nonclassical replicator-mutator partial differential equation. We show that eleven distinct evolutionarily stable states can arise, depending on the mutation regime and the shape of fitness trade-offs between male and female functions. Remarkably, most reproductive systems described in the literature emerge as limiting or stationary distributions of our model. We further show that mutation alone can drive shifts between reproductive systems by recurrently introducing variants with suboptimal resource allocation, thereby preventing populations from remaining indefinitely at classical evolutionarily stable strategies.
